query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In T91-type ferritic/martensitic steels used in aggressive chemical and nuclear environments, a dual-oxide protective system—composed of an inner Si‐rich oxide layer that promotes the formation of an outer Cr‐rich (or mixed Cr/Al) oxide—is most effectively established in steels with an optimized (intermediate) grain size. This balance minimizes oxygen and metal ion diffusion. In overly coarse grains the oxide films form slowly and in overly fine grains they become discontinuous due to excessive grain boundary area; thus, an intermediate grain refinement combined with moderate (≈1.3 wt%) silicon addition yields a continuous, stable oxide film and, consequently, superior corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: T91 ferritic/martensitic steel produced with controlled thermomechanical processing to yield distinct grain size distributions (coarse, intermediate, ultrafine) and alloyed with varying Si contents (e.g., 0.5, 1.3, and 2.0 wt%).
generation.intervention: Apply specific thermomechanical treatments to vary the grain size while adjusting Si content; then expose the samples to liquid lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE) environments (or liquid lead) at 550 °C with controlled oxygen levels under both static and dynamic conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (around 550 °C) LBE or lead environments with controlled oxygen partial pressures that simulate chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions. Both static and dynamic exposure regimes should be tested.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain size governs oxide film continuity and thickness, while silicon addition promotes the formation of a dense, Si-rich inner oxide that assists in catalyzing a continuous outer Cr-rich (or mixed oxide) layer. An optimized microstructure (neither too coarse nor excessively refined) mediates the formation and stability of the protective dual-layer oxide.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen and alloying element diffusion during high-temperature exposure leads to oxidation. Moderate Si content favors the preferential formation of a Si-rich inner oxide that acts as a diffusion barrier; this barrier, in turn, assists the rapid formation and maintenance of an outer Cr-rich protective film. However, if the grain size is too fine, the high density of grain boundaries may disrupt oxide continuity by accelerating metal dissolution, while coarse grains delay uniform oxide formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels processed to have an intermediate grain size and alloyed with approximately 1.3 wt% Si will form a more continuous and stable dual-oxide film, as shown by thinner, more uniform oxide layers and reduced corrosion depths, compared to coarse-grained or ultrafine-grained samples and those with lower Si content.
generation.baseline: T91 steel with low Si content (e.g., 0.5 wt%) and coarse grain structure—expected to form a less protective, inhomogeneous oxide film resulting in higher corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: These effects are expected to hold in high-temperature liquid metal environments (e.g., LBE at ~550 °C) with controlled oxygen levels typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions; extrapolation to very different environments (e.g., low-temperature aqueous systems or high-irradiation conditions) should be made with caution.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from studies on oxide film formation in T91 and 9Cr-based steels (e.g., evidence from PMC10054900 and PMC9028533) and integrates insights on the role of grain size from studies on austenitic stainless steels (e.g., PMC6702197) to propose a combined effect of silicon alloying and microstructural tailoring. The quantitative boundaries for optimal grain size and precise Si thresholds remain uncertain, and effects under simultaneous irradiation have not been addressed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of T91 samples with three targeted silicon contents (e.g., 0.5, 1.3, and 2.0 wt%) and process each set to attain three distinct grain sizes (coarse, intermediate, ultrafine) via tailored thermomechanical routes. Expose all samples to an LBE environment at 550 °C under both static and dynamic oxygen-controlled conditions for predetermined durations (e.g., 500 and 1000 hours). Post-exposure, assess the oxide layer morphology, continuity, and corrosion penetration using SEM, TEM, EPMA, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Elemental composition and continuity of oxide layers (using EPMA/XPS)
Corrosion depths and rates (quantified by cross-sectional analysis and weight loss measurements)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (to assess film resistivity and protective behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with intermediate grain size and approximately 1.3 wt% Si do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide film continuity, reduced oxide growth kinetics, and lower corrosion depth compared to both the coarse (low Si) baseline and the ultrafine-grained variants—or if either the ultrafine grains or different Si contents unexpectedly outperform the intermediate condition—then the hypothesis regarding the necessity of an optimized grain size with moderate Si addition for the protective oxide formation would be falsified.

The effect of grain size, prior deformation and deformation rate on the corrosion behavior of AISI 321 austenitic stainless steel in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was determined. The as-received coarse-grained alloy (~37 µm grain size) was subjected to thermomechanical processing to develop fine (~3 µm grain size) and ultrafine (~0.24 µm grain size) grained structure. The coarse, fine and ultrafine grained specimens were deformed under dynamic (8.8 × 103 s−1) and quasi-static (4.4 × 10−3 s−1) loading conditions to the same true strain of ~0.86 using a split Hopkinson pressure bar and Instron R5500 mechanical testing systems, respectively. Using XRD, SEM, TEM, EBSD, and EDS characterization techniques to investigate the steel specimens, the following conclusions are drawn; Corrosion resistance is highest in the UFG specimens, followed by FG and CG specimens, in that order. This is due to the formation of a more stable adsorbed passive film in UFG specimens. The corrosion resistance of AISI 321 austenitic stainless steel follows the order: quasi-static > dynamic > undeformed, for all grain sizes. The corrosion failure modes of materials in LBE are oxidation and dissolution, and the root cause is diffusion. On the one hand, the matrix material diffuses into LBE, on the other hand, oxygen diffuses into the matrix. The corrosion mechanism and oxide film behavior of 9–12% Cr steel in LBR were studied, and a more classical oxide film growth model was put forward []. In this study, the change of oxide film after the addition of Si is studied, the formation sequence of oxide film in different layers is analyzed from the perspective of the formation energy of various oxides, and a new model is proposed. Excessively high oxygen content in LBE will produce a thick oxide film which can protect the material from further corrosion, but the falling off of the oxide film is easy to block the flow channel, thus affecting the reactor operation. It is hard to form a continuous oxide film in the oxygen-depleted LBE solution, so that the matrix cannot be protected from corrosion. Therefore, the ideal oxygen content in the alloy is of great significance for improving the corrosion resistance of structural materials in LBE.
